rewrites.summary:
A July 2026 national data analysis places Georgia’s recorded killing rate for trans women at 4.8 per 100k per year — among the country’s highest — but that figure sits at or near the region’s general homicide baseline: the general US murder rate is single-digit per 100k, with Georgia’s already elevated against the national average. Calibrated that way, it reads as an elevated version of a normal, otherwise non-trans-specific risk rather than an organised anti-trans campaign — serious, but proportioned — and a state law-review series adds that the long-run fatality record concentrates around Atlanta (at least 15 fatal cases statewide 1990–2014, 11 in Atlanta; 16 more 2015–2023, 8 in Atlanta). Both series are acknowledged undercount floors, and that uncertainty cuts both ways: the real rate could be higher. The analysis’s own warning is that a legal-risk grade describes how the state behaves, not how its people do.

For a trans visitor specifically, Georgia has no facility or bathroom restriction, no criminalisation of same-sex conduct, and no document-marker exposure regime — traveller-relevant positives that keep ground-level legal exposure low on those axes. The state’s care restrictions are mostly resident- and family-facing climate signals with limited direct effect on adult trans visitors: the minors-care ban (in force since 1 July 2023) constrains providers treating under-18 patients, and the February 2025 Savannah cancellation of adult gender-affirming surgeries narrows in-state care-seekers’ options rather than the legal position of a visiting adult.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: National policy turbulence and litigation flux colour the picture: the health centre’s 13 February 2025 cancellation of adult gender-affirming surgeries was attributed to state and national law in terms that appear to reference the 28 January 2025 national executive order denying Medicare and Medicaid funding to providers of youth gender-transition care; a national court settlement (October 2023) requires the state’s public-employee health plan to pay for medically necessary gender-affirming care for employees, spouses and dependents after a December 2022 lawsuit, and could fund such care for minors outside the state even though it is prohibited inside it; and the minors-care ban, signed 23 March 2023, drew a promised lawsuit from the state’s civil-liberties organisation.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Resident discrimination record: in April 2023 Atlanta police were actively investigating three violent crimes against transgender women that year — two Black transgender women were fatally shot a week apart, and a January 2023 shooting that left a transgender woman in critical condition remained open; the department itself acknowledged the “epidemic-level violence” Black and brown transgender women face.

The care measures are resident- and family-facing. The minors-care ban (signed 23 March 2023, in force since 1 July 2023) bars licensed medical professionals from providing patients under 18 with hormone therapy or surgery related to gender transition, carries possible licence revocation, and lets minors who began hormone replacement therapy before 1 July 2023 continue. Adult-care access has shrunk for residents: a medical centre in Savannah cancelled all gender-affirming surgeries on 13 February 2025 — including a pre-approved double mastectomy for a 24-year-old transgender man — and a community group said at least two other Savannah-area residents were also denied care. Public-employee coverage, by contrast, continued under the October 2023 settlement.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Both killing-count series — the 4.8 per 100k rate and the 1990–2014 / 2015–2023 case counts — are acknowledged undercount floors, so the true totals and the true rate for trans women are unknown; the uncertainty cuts both ways, and the real rate could be higher. The 13 February 2025 surgery cancellation was attributed to state and national law, but the link to the 28 January 2025 national funding order is reported as an appearance (“appears to reference”) rather than a published explanation from the medical centre. The record contains no border-screening or document-procedure information for visitors, so document conditions on the ground remain unverified beyond what is recorded above.
rewrites.notes: Rule-8 re-calibration: the 4.8 per 100k killing rate re-framed against the US/Georgia general homicide baseline (single-digit per 100k; Georgia's general rate elevated vs the national average) as an elevated version of a normal, otherwise non-trans-specific risk — serious but proportioned, not a campaign; the undercount caveat retained and made two-sided (real rates could be higher); the law-review case series (15 statewide 1990–2014 / 11 Atlanta; 16 more 2015–2023 / 8 Atlanta) kept as the street-violence evidence. Rule-6/rule-1 traveller lens added: no facility or bathroom restriction, no same-sex criminalisation and no document-marker exposure regime for visitors stated as traveller-relevant positives (previously absent from the summary). Minors-care ban and adult-surgery shrinkage moved mostly to localsOnly as resident/family-facing climate signals; the summary now states their limited direct effect on adult trans visitors. Rule-6 split kept: tangentialFactors = national policy flux (funding-order/Savannah link, October 2023 settlement, minors-ban lawsuit); localsOnly = resident discrimination record, Atlanta police violence, care-coverage saga; outOfScopeNotes = undercount uncertainty, the 'appears to reference' attribution caveat, unverified document conditions. All facts and dates (4.8 per 100k, 1 July 2023, 23 March 2023, 13 February 2025, October 2023, December 2022, 28 January 2025) retained from the existing record text and sources; the only new input is the general-homicide calibration baseline supplied in the task directive.
